title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling Playbook, Benchmarking Suite, Runbooks and Known Issues
author: Asha Patel
content:
Overview

This document consolidates the runtime architecture, kernel scheduling heuristics, profiling playbooks, the canonical benchmarking suite, release notes summary, known issues, and operational runbooks for Redwood Inference serving runtime. It is intended as the single-pane reference for engineers and SREs who operate or modify the serving runtime.

Goals
- Describe how kernel selection and scheduling interact with batching, KV cache, and quantized execution paths.
- Provide repeatable profiling steps and a lightweight playbook for performance investigations.
- Define the benchmarking suite, workloads, and acceptance criteria for releases.
- Provide concise runbooks for common operational incidents.

1) Runtime architecture (summary)

High-level components
- Frontend/API router: request validation, tenant routing, and deadline enforcement.
- Orchestration layer: policy-based routing (latency/cost/region), model variant resolution, and autoscaler interface.
- Serving runtime (worker): GPU-backed inference process that manages: model loading, KV cache, kernel selection, continuous batching, and IO.
- Sidecars: metrics exporter, prometheus client, local cache manager, and controlled diagnostics agent.
- Control plane: model versioning, rollout manager, and centralized config distribution.

Sequence of a request
1. Request received and validated by API router.
2. Routing policy selects cluster/pool and model variant.
3. Worker process assigns to a scheduling slot and (optionally) attaches to an in-memory KV cache.
4. Kernel selection occurs based on model architecture, sequence length, data type (fp16/int8), and current GPU occupancy.
5. Continuous batching aggregator adds request to a micro-batch and dispatches kernels.
6. Output is assembled, post-processed, and streamed to client.

Key invariants and SLOs
- P95 end-to-end latency SLOs (typical):
  - Small models (<=2B params): 40ms P95 for 16-token requests.
  - Medium models (2B-13B): 120ms P95 for 32-token requests.
  - Large models (>=70B): 700ms P95 for 64-token requests (depends on model variant and quantization).
- Throughput SLOs: tokens/sec targets per GPU are maintained per-profile in the model catalog.
- Error budget and fallback policy: on repeated latency breaches, requests are automatically routed to a compatible lower-cost variant (fallback).

2) Kernel selection and scheduling heuristics

Kernel selection inputs
- Model architecture type (transformer decoder, encoder-decoder)
- Attention implementation availability (flash-attn v2, Triton kernels, CUTLASS, fused kernels)
- Data type: fp32, fp16, bf16, int8/NTK8 quantized paths
- Sequence length distribution and prefix reuse rate
- Hardware capabilities: H100 tensor-core shape support, A100 SM counts, memory bandwidth, L2 cache sizes

Heuristic rules (high level)
- If sequence length < 128 and model uses causal attention, prefer fused flash-attn kernels (low latency) when available.
- For long sequences (>512) or models with substantial kv-cache reuse, prefer KV-optimized kernels that minimize memory copies and leverage persistent memory.
- If GPU occupancy < 40% and tail latency is critical, opt for single-request optimized kernels (reduce batch-merging).
- For high throughput (latency-tolerant) workloads, favor large batch kernel paths with CUTLASS/Triton autotuned matmul.
- For quantized models, route to quantization-aware kernels with dequantize/accumulate paths to avoid numerical regressions.

Kernel selection flow (simplified)
1. Gather runtime signals: current occupancy, median seq length, prefix hit rate, and memory headroom.
2. Look up model profile in the catalog (preferred kernels, fallback kernels, quantization profile).
3. Run a light-weight cost model estimate (latency vs tokens/sec) and pick the kernel family.
4. If estimate predicts SLA breach, try alternative: change batch window, lower precision, or fallback variant.

3) Profiling playbook (how-to)

Principles
- Start with low-overhead telemetry: GPU and application metrics, logs, and traces. Only escalate to intrusive profilers for a root-cause.
- Reproduce with the canonical benchmarking suite and a production-like input set whenever possible.

Telemetry checklist (quick)
- Prometheus dashboards: GPU utilization, GPU memory, kernel latency, batch size distribution, queue depth.
- Tracing: request path trace including model load, batching delay, and kernel dispatch timestamps.
- Logs: worker stderr, model loader logs, and occlusion/fallback events.

Light-touch investigation steps
1. Validate the SLO breach on dashboards: verify p50/p95/p99 for the last 15/60/180 minutes.
2. Check GPU utilization and memory: high GPU util with high latency indicates kernel-level stalls; low GPU util with high latency indicates scheduling/backpressure or blocked IO.
3. Check batch size distribution: sudden increase in very small batches increases tail latency.
4. Inspect recent deployments and model rollouts: model change or quantization flip often coincides with regression.

Deep profiling (when needed)
- When to run: persistent regression (>30m) after light-touch checks, or suspected kernel-level inefficiency.
- Tools and commands:
  - nsys (NVIDIA Nsight Systems): capture end-to-end timeline. Example: nsys profile -o /tmp/trace --trace=nvtx,cuda --sample=cpu ./run_inference_load_test.sh
  - ncu (NVIDIA Nsight Compute): kernel-level metrics. Example: ncu --target-processes=all --export sqlite --set full ./worker_process
  - triton/torch-torch.profiler or runtime-internal microprofiler for CUDA kernel timing when using Triton-based matmuls.
  - nvprof is deprecated; avoid for H100 stacks.
- Recommended profile capture window: 30s-120s under steady-state load.

Interpreting profiles
- Identify long kernel times relative to expected baseline and correlate with parameters: M, K, N shapes.
- Look for launch latency spikes (CPU scheduling), memory copies (H2D/D2H), and excessive synchronization (cudaDeviceSynchronize) calls.
- For multi-tenant GPU nodes, confirm no noisy neighbor via CUDA MPS or MIG interference (on H100).

4) Benchmarking suite (canonical and repeatable)

Purpose
- Provide reproducible measurements for releases, model onboarding, and capacity planning.

Benchmark components
- Workload generator: supports chat (multi-turn), streaming, and embeddings. Configurable token-length distributions and concurrent client counts.
- Dataset: representative prompts sets (LLM-bench-small, chat-cases, long-context tests) stored in the infra bucket.
- Collector: collects p50/p95/p99 latencies, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, memory use, and cost model estimates.
- Analysis: scripts to produce release-ready tables and plots.

Canonical test matrix (examples)
| Model Variant | Hardware | Precision | Seq len | Concurrency | Acceptance criteria |
| gpt-small-v1 | A100-40GB | fp16 | 32 | 64 clients | p95 < 120ms, tokens/sec >= 50k |
| gpt-medium-v2 | H100-80GB | fp16/bf16 | 64 | 32 clients | p95 < 300ms, tokens/sec >= 30k |
| llm-large-quant | A100-80GB | int8 | 256 | 8 clients | p95 < 900ms, accuracy regression < 1.5% |

Running benchmarks (short recipe)
1. Reserve a clean pool: use dedicated benchmark cluster with no other tenants.
2. Load target model variant and pin kernel config to ensure repeatability.
3. Run warmup for 5 minutes to populate KV cache.
4. Execute the workload generator for 10 minutes steady-state per test.
5. Collect output, validate against acceptance criteria, and store artifacts in the benchmark run directory.

Artifacts to store
- raw metrics (Prometheus exports), profile captures (nsys/ncu), and summary CSV/JSON.

5) Release notes (serving-runtime highlights)

This section documents the recent runtime release highlights and behavioral changes that operators should know. Add short entries per release and link to PRs.

Release 2028-11-30 (v5.3.0)
- Added dynamic kernel cost estimator and heuristics for mixed-precision fallback.
- Improved KV cache serialization to reduce cold-start model-load time by ~18%.
- New benchmark profiles for H100 tensor-core tiling shapes.

Release 2028-09-15 (v5.2.1)
- Fixed race condition in batch aggregator causing occasional zero-length batches.
- Backported improved Triton matmul autotuner to fp16 paths.

Operational impact notes
- v5.3.0 enables a new config key runtime.kernel_cost_estimator with default enabled; turning this off retains legacy kernel selection.
- When rolling out v5.3.0, monitor p99 latencies closely for the first 60 minutes after a region rollout.

6) Known issues and mitigations

1) Intermittent p99 spikes on H100-optimized kernels
- Symptom: p99 spikes without corresponding util increase.
- Cause: occasionally suboptimal kernel tiling selected by the autotuner for certain M/N shapes.
- Mitigation: pin kernel tile in model profile to known-good tiling or disable autotuner for the affected pool.
- Permanent fix: tracked in ticket RUNTIME-4871.

2) KV cache deserialization stalls during cold start
- Symptom: model load takes >30s occasionally after restarts.
- Cause: synchronous serialization on load path blocks worker.
- Mitigation: enable async_deserialize: true in the model profile and pre-warm cache during deploys.

3) Quantized path numerical regressions for rare tokens
- Symptom: accuracy drop on specific prompt sets after int8 rollout.
- Cause: quantization calibration mismatch for out-of-distribution tokens.
- Mitigation: run local calibration on realistic prompt set; if regression > 1.5% revert to fp16 variant.

4) OOMs on mixed workloads
- Symptom: occasional OOM killing the worker process during high-concurrency tests.
- Mitigation: reduce max_concurrency per worker, add eviction policy for largest batches, or increase memory buffer pool.

7) Runtime runbooks (concise playbooks for incidents)

Runbook A: High latency (p95/p99 breaches)
1. Triage (0-5 min)
   - Check the latency dashboard for affected region/pool and timeframe.
   - Identify whether CPU, GPU, or scheduling is the bottleneck.
   - If slope is sudden and coincides with deploy, roll back the model variant or runtime version to previous stable version.
2. Immediate mitigations (5-15 min)
   - Increase worker pool size (scale up) or shift traffic to lower-latency region if policy allows.
   - Temporarily disable autotuner (runtime.kernel_cost_estimator=false) to lock kernel choices.
3. Deep investigation (15-90 min)
   - Run nsys trace on a representative node with a captured workload.
   - Check batch size histogram and queue depth metrics.
   - Engage on-call runtime engineer.
4. Post-incident
   - Record timeline, root cause, and actions in incident tracker.
   - Add regression test to benchmark suite if relevant.

Runbook B: GPU OOM / Worker crash
1. Triage (0-5 min)
   - Check node events and worker logs for OOM messages.
   - Confirm model memory footprint and concurrent batch sizes.
2. Immediate mitigation (5-15 min)
   - Restart the worker (kubectl rollout restart or restart process) onto a node with more headroom.
   - If repeated, scale down max_concurrency and enable batch_eviction_policy: LRU.
3. Investigation (15-120 min)
   - Reproduce with benchmark generator and memory profiler.
   - Validate kernel allocation and pinned memory pools.

Runbook C: Degraded accuracy after quantized rollout
1. Triage
   - Compare evaluations against baseline prompt set.
   - If regression > 1.5%, revert traffic to fp16 variant.
2. Mitigation
   - Re-run quantization calibration with expanded calibration set.
   - If calibration fails, label model variant as blocked and notify product and ML lead.

8) Team wiki and ownership

Ownership
- Primary: serving-runtime team (runtime-infra subteam).
- Secondary: applied-ml-and-evals (for quantization calibration and eval prompts).
- On-call rotation: see /confluence/eng-sre/oncall-roster (link maintained by SRE).

Documentation pointers
- Model catalog: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/model-onboarding (profiles and kernel pins).
- Benchmark artifacts: infra://benchmarks/serving-runtime (internal storage).
- SRE dashboards: Grafana/serving-runtime-overview (p95/p99, tokens/sec, GPU health).

9) Checklist for making changes to kernel scheduling or autotuner
1. Add unit tests for cost estimator logic.
2. Add a benchmark run using the canonical suite (compare p50/p95/p99 and tokens/sec).
3. Roll out behind a feature flag and monitor automatically for 60m per region.
4. Revert quickly if p99 regression > 10% or accuracy regression > 1%.

Appendix A: Useful commands and snippets
- Check GPU processes: nvidia-smi --query-compute-apps=pid,process_name,used_gpu_memory --format=csv
- Capture nsight systems trace: nsys profile -o /tmp/trace --trace=nvtx,cuda --sample=cpu ./scripts/run_bench.sh
- Lightweight batch histogram: curl http://metrics.internal/serving/runtime/batch_hist | jq '.'
